A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Otter research work. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained methods, tables, figures, and prompts can be matched reliably across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments with GPT-4o and Mistral-large, evaluations on TDD-Bench-Verified and SWT-Lite, component ablations, and filtering of patches from 22 SWE systems.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds planner ablations, sampling comparisons, test diagnostics, and a patch-ranking experiment.

M1.justification: The localizer, self-reflective planner, test generator, import repair, and five-prompt Otter++ selection procedure are unchanged. The appendix prompts are retained verbatim apart from numbering. Added experimental variants do not replace the proposed pipeline.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 449 TDD-Bench-Verified instances across 12 Python repositories and 276 SWT-Lite instances. V2 Section 6.7 adds a downstream task: selecting among patches from the top three leaderboard systems using CodeT ranking, extending the earlier patch-filtering application.

E2.justification: The six external comparison methods in Table 3 and the 22-system patch-filtering roster remain unchanged. V2 Table 10 expands the internal ensemble comparison with greedy/high-temperature and heterogeneous/high-temperature mixtures. Newly discussed EvoCoder and CodeMonkeys are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V2 adds one-to-five-candidate scaling, temperature-1.0 sampling, mixed ten-candidate evaluation, and a one-attempt planner control. The original principal evaluation settings remain unchanged. Section 6.4 also revises the stated inputs of two comparison methods from a golden patch to a proposed patch; this changes the reported setting without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands analysis beyond v1's component-removal and contamination studies. Table 2 separately tests plan refinement and action validation; Table 6 diagnoses outcomes by test modification, execution failure, and localization correctness. Appendices C–E add ensemble scaling, temperature-versus-prompt comparisons, oracle-ranking analysis, and hallucination-replacement diagnostics.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run uncertainty estimates. Table 10's multiple generated candidates and their average performance describe ensemble sampling, rather than replications estimating experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: The headline Otter and Otter++ results remain unchanged, but substantial new results accompany the added analyses and Table 1 coverage column. For example, Table 10 reports 166 versus 146 Top-1 successes for heterogeneous prompts versus high-temperature sampling. Table 1 corrects the GPT-4o zero-shot count from 99 to 84 while retaining 18.7%. Section 6.7 additionally reports a sparsely documented 2% patch-ranking improvement.

T1.justification: V1 only describes tddScore as blending fail-to-pass performance with coverage. V2 Section 5.3 adds explicit mathematical definitions of dataset aggregation, fail-to-pass correctness, and adequacy over added and deleted lines. This formalizes the custom metric already used in v1; it does not establish a changed metric or introduce proofs.

C1.justification: V1 attributes TDD-Bench-Verified to the authors' prior work. V2 presents it as a contribution of this paper in the abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion. This substantially expands the claimed contribution scope, while retaining the central Otter performance and SWE-patch-validation claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations connecting test modification to available context, comparative performance to execution feedback and output-format demands, and ensemble gains to prompt diversity rather than ranking alone. It also discusses limits to scaling and improving already-ranked leaderboard patches. The original limitations concerning Python coverage, single-test generation, and unreliable SymPy coverage remain unchanged.

D1.justification: New Section 5 substantially improves benchmark documentation: it specifies the evaluation harness, execution of contributed tests, filtering from 500 to 449 instances, and coverage computation. These are disclosures about the retained benchmark, not evidence of changed construction. V2 also identifies GPT-4 for Table 3 comparators and explicitly states that generated tests are available through the existing repository.

R1.justification: V2 removes the Ahmed et al. benchmark reference and changes TDD-Bench-Verified from prior work into a present-paper contribution, materially revising research positioning. It also adds substantive discussions of EvoCoder, CodeT, CodeMonkeys, and SWE-Bench+, including their relationship to Otter and its evaluation.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the relative order of retained sections remain intact. V2 inserts a dedicated benchmark section and three analysis appendices, makes localized wording corrections, and expands related-work, comparison, and impact explanations. The revision mainly adds material rather than extensively rewriting the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds benchmark-filtering and evaluation-harness diagrams, plus four analysis tables. Table 1 gains a coverage column, and Table 2 gains component grouping and additional ablation rows. Existing graphical content and prompt figures are retained, with substantial resizing, relocation, and surrounding layout changes.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens auditability and evidence for the central design choices. It makes the previously only briefly described benchmark evaluation and score self-contained, isolates refinement and validation within the novel planner, and quantitatively tests heterogeneous prompting against temperature sampling. It also fixes the inconsistent zero-shot count. The new 2% patch-ranking claim remains underspecified, but the stronger documentation and targeted validation provide substantial benefits independently of that claim.
